_about: Explanations in our own words, each checked against its source on the date given with it. Map abbreviations are from the National Library of Scotland's list compiled by Dr Richard Oliver; many have several meanings, and the map's context decides which.

terms.meaning: The main unit of British money before 1971, divided into 20 shillings (240 pence). The £ sign comes from the Latin libra.

sources.title: University of Nottingham, Manuscripts and Special Collections: Money

terms.meaning: One twentieth of a pound, divided into 12 pence. Written 's'; also called a 'bob'.

terms.meaning: One twelfth of a shilling, divided into two halfpennies or four farthings. Written 'd', from the Latin denarius.

terms.meaning: How amounts were written before 1971, e.g. £1 9s 6d or £1.9.6. Shillings and pence alone could be written 9s 6d or 9/6, said 'nine and six'. Britain changed to decimal currency on 15 February 1971.

terms.meaning: From 1834, parishes in England and Wales were grouped into poor law unions to run poor relief together, reporting to the new Poor Law Commission. To find a union's records you usually need to know its name.

sources.title: The National Archives research guide: Poverty and the Poor Laws

terms.meaning: The body that ran a poor law union, elected by ratepayers from the union's parishes.

sources.title: The National Archives research guide: Poverty and the Poor Laws

terms.meaning: From the Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834, parishes in England and Wales were combined into poor law unions, each with its own workhouse. A board of guardians, elected by ratepayers, ran each union, and a workhouse master and matron managed the workhouse day to day. Poor law unions continued until 1930.

sources.title: The National Archives research guide: Workhouse inmates and staff
The National Archives research guide: Poverty and the Poor Laws

terms.before: Before 1834 the poor laws were mostly run by each parish, under local magistrates, so a workhouse or poorhouse mentioned before then was a parish one, not a union workhouse.
terms.may_mean: A workhouse record shows the poor law was supporting someone at that time. People went into workhouses for many different reasons and for different lengths of time; this record alone doesn't say why they were there.

where_to_look.text: Admission and discharge books, and registers of births, baptisms and deaths, kept by the workhouse. They're at the local or county archive, and not all survive.

sources.title: The National Archives research guide: Workhouse inmates and staff

where_to_look.text: The census, 1841 to 1921, which can show who was in a workhouse on census night.

sources.title: The National Archives research guide: Workhouse inmates and staff

where_to_look.text: Poor law union correspondence at The National Archives (MH 12), which sometimes names individual paupers. Correspondence from 24 unions, 1834 to 1871, is catalogued in detail and online.

sources.title: The National Archives research guide: Workhouse inmates and staff

where_to_look.text: You usually need the name of the poor law union, which may differ from the town the workhouse was in: Eton union's workhouse was in Slough.

sources.title: The National Archives research guide: Poverty and the Poor Laws

terms.meaning: The parish responsible for a poor person, generally their parish of birth. Disputes over which parish had to pay could end up at quarter sessions.

sources.title: The National Archives research guide: Poverty and the Poor Laws

terms.meaning: A statement made to justices of the peace by someone whose parish of settlement was in doubt. They often describe a person's life and work.

sources.title: The National Archives research guide: Poverty and the Poor Laws

terms.meaning: Before 1834, poor relief was mostly run locally by each parish. Overseers of the poor, with the churchwardens, kept the parish's poor accounts.

sources.title: The National Archives research guide: Poverty and the Poor Laws

terms.meaning: Great Britain changed from the Julian to the Gregorian calendar in September 1752. 2 September 1752 was followed straight away by 14 September, so eleven days were lost. Dates written before the change are in the older calendar, so they don't line up exactly with today's.

sources.title: University of Nottingham, Manuscripts and Special Collections: Julian and Gregorian calendars

terms.meaning: Until 1751, England and Wales counted each year as starting on Lady Day, 25 March; 1752 was the first year to start on 1 January. So a date between 1 January and 24 March before then belongs to the year we'd now call the next one, and is often written with both years, like 25 January 1748/9. Scotland started the year on 1 January from 1600.

sources.title: University of Nottingham, Manuscripts and Special Collections: Historical and civil years

terms.meaning: The four days on which rents were traditionally paid in England, each a church feast: Lady Day (25 March), Midsummer Day (24 June), Michaelmas (29 September) and Christmas Day (25 December). Rent due 'at Michaelmas' was due on 29 September.

sources.title: University of Nottingham, Manuscripts and Special Collections: Feast days

terms.meaning: Many documents are dated by the year of the reigning monarch rather than the calendar year, usually counted from the day they came to the throne. For example, 1 Henry V ran from 21 March 1413 to 20 March 1414, so one regnal year spans parts of two calendar years. To convert one you need the monarch's accession date, which handbooks of dates list.

sources.title: University of Nottingham, Manuscripts and Special Collections: Regnal years

terms.meaning: A public announcement in church that a couple intend to marry, giving anyone the chance to say why the marriage can't lawfully take place. In the Church of England today, banns are read on three Sundays in the three months before the wedding, in the parish where each of the couple lives and in the church where they marry. A banns entry shows a marriage was planned; look for the marriage itself to confirm it happened.

sources.title: Church of England: Reading of banns

terms.meaning: Probate is a court's approval of a will; once granted, the will is said to be 'proved' and the executor (the person named to carry out its wishes) can act. In England and Wales, until 12 January 1858, wills were proved by church and other courts. The most important was the Prerogative Court of Canterbury, covering the south of England and most of Wales; the Prerogative Court of York covered the north.

sources.title: The National Archives research guide: Wills 1384–1858

terms.meaning: The smallest land division in Ireland: counties are divided into baronies, baronies into civil parishes, and parishes into townlands, an ancient division older than the parishes and counties. There are about 62,000 townlands in Ireland and over 9,000 in Northern Ireland, from a few acres to several thousand. Land was let by townland, and the Tithe Applotment Books, censuses and valuations used them, so Irish records are usually arranged by townland. Spellings vary a lot, because Irish names were written down in English.

sources.title: Public Record Office of Northern Ireland: Local History 1, The Townland

terms.meaning: In poor law records, someone being supported by the poor law. Before 1834 a pauper was a charge on their parish of settlement, generally the parish where they were born (for a married woman, her husband's parish of birth).
terms.may_mean: It describes their situation when the record was made, not their whole life.

where_to_look.text: Before 1834: the parish overseers' accounts, vestry minute books and settlement examinations, at the local or county archive.

sources.title: The National Archives research guide: Poverty and the Poor Laws
The National Archives research guide: Poverty and the Poor Laws

terms.meaning: Workhouses kept admission and discharge books recording people coming in and leaving. With the workhouse's registers of births, baptisms and deaths, they're the main records of individual inmates.
terms.may_mean: An admission date and a discharge date show when someone was in the workhouse, not why they came in or where they went next.

where_to_look.text: The workhouse's own registers at the local or county archive (not all survive), and the census for anyone there on census night.

sources.title: The National Archives research guide: Workhouse inmates and staff
The National Archives research guide: Workhouse inmates and staff

terms.meaning: Before 1834, if two parishes disagreed about which was responsible for a poor person (their place of settlement), the dispute could go to quarter sessions.
terms.may_mean: A settlement dispute shows parishes disagreeing over who was responsible for someone's relief.

where_to_look.text: Quarter sessions records and settlement examinations, at the local or county archive.
